newsitem.title: USA: U.S. power industry detects no solar disruptions.
newsitem.headline: U.S. power industry detects no solar disruptions.

text.p: Despite warnings a solar storm might disrupt the North American power grid, U.S. electric industry officials said Thursday there were no signs their systems had been affected.

Gene Gorzelnik, director of communications at the North American Electric Reliability Council (NERC) in Princeton, N.J., said none of the council's 10 member regions had reported geomagnetic disturbances resulting from the storm.
"It looks like it was a non-event," he said. "All monitoring devices showed readings well below levels that would require preemptive action."

The warning was sounded Wednesday by the U.S. National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) when it said ionized particles from a major solar storm, spotted by satellite Monday, might hit the Earth's magnetic field sometime late Wednesday or Thursday.

NASA officials said the impact, while undetectable and harmless to humans, could trigger so-called geomagnetic disturbances in the earth's surface, disrupting power generation and transmission systems if severe enough.
A solar storm triggered a huge power outage in Canada on March 13, 1989, tripping Hydro Quebec's power grid and leaving the entire province of Quebec and its five million residents without power.
Industry officials said the warning system currently in place is still in its infancy and despite Wednesday's alarm, is a valuable asset to the industry.

"It's much better to know it's coming than not to. There are things we can do, and we'll take reasonable precautions," said Jeff Williams, a spokesman for the Mid-Atlantic Area Council (MAAC), a NERC member whose territory covers New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Maryland.

The main precautions include heightened monitoring of ground currents and, if needed, trimming power generation to lighten loads on transmission lines, making it easier to regulate possible voltage surges and protect sensitive electro-magnetic equipment.

Scientists following the solar cloud said late Wednesday it would likely miss Earth, a judgement they were unable to make earlier in the day as the particles raced across space at about 1.5 million miles per hour (2.4 million kph).
